# The research question

Empirical psychology rests on samples, and the credibility of a finding depends
in part on who was sampled. When an article omits the demographic composition of
its participants, readers cannot judge the scope of the claim, and downstream
meta-analyses cannot assess who the literature actually speaks for. This is the
question of sample representativeness, and it has both a descriptive and a
temporal dimension.

This project addresses both. First, at what rate do psychology articles report
participant demographics (gender, race, education, and socioeconomic status)?
Second, has that reporting rate shifted over the period 2010 to 2026, and does
the trajectory differ across subfields or across the disruption of the COVID-19
pandemic?

We restrict attention to a single venue, PLOS ONE, for methodological
tractability. It is high-volume, multidisciplinary, and fully open access, which
means the entire corpus is retrievable and machine-readable rather than locked
behind subscription paywalls. That combination is what makes a corpus-scale study
of tens of thousands of articles feasible rather than a hand-coded sample of a
few hundred.

Because manual coding does not scale to that volume, the design delegates the
reading to a large language model. For each qualifying article, the model reads
the methods text and returns the reported demographics in a fixed structured
form, which we then aggregate into reporting-rate trends.

## Temporal design

To characterize change over time we partition the study window into four periods
chosen to reflect substantively distinct eras:

| Stage | Years | Rationale |
|-------|-------|-----------|
| Early | 2010 to 2014 | Baseline era |
| Middle | 2015 to 2019 | Settled, pre-pandemic |
| COVID | 2020 to 2023 | Pandemic disruption |
| Post-COVID | 2024 to 2026 | Recovery |

# The extraction schema

For every distinct participant sample an article describes, we code whether, and
in how much detail, each demographic was reported. The coding scheme is taken
directly from the project brief:

| Demographic | Coded fields |
|-------------|--------------|
| Gender | Reported (yes/no) plus the percentage breakdown (male / female / other) |
| Race | Reported (yes/no) plus the percentage breakdown (white / black / hispanic / asian / other) |
| Education | Reported (yes/no) plus the percentage with versus without college |
| Socioeconomic status | An ordinal 0/1/2 code: 0 = not reported, 1 = reported only categorically (e.g. "low income"), 2 = reported with a numeric threshold (e.g. below $30,000) |

Two features of the schema are deliberate and consequential.

The unit of analysis is the participant sample, not the article. A single article
may report several independent samples, and each is coded as its own record,
keyed to the shared article identifier (its DOI). Collapsing an article's samples
into one record would discard genuine within-article variation and bias the
reporting-rate estimates.

Each record also carries article-level metadata: publication date, the
corresponding author's institution, and the full PLOS subject taxonomy for the
article. These support subgroup analysis and provenance tracking.

## Inclusion criteria

An article enters the corpus only if it is an empirical research article (not an
editorial, correction, or review), published in PLOS ONE, classified by PLOS
under psychology (any subfield), and dated between 2010 and 2026. No lower bound
is placed on sample size, per the brief.

# Pipeline architecture

The system is a linear sequence of stages, each materializing an artifact the
next stage consumes:

```
1. Enumerate qualifying psychology articles  ->  master index (58,467 articles)  [DONE]
2. Draw a stratified pilot sample            ->  46 articles                      [DONE]
3. Run the model over the pilot              ->  extracted demographics            [NEXT]
4. Manually adjudicate pilot accuracy        ->  proceed / revise decision
5. Run the model over the full index         ->  full demographics table
6. Aggregate the table                       ->  reporting-rate trends (the result)
```

Stages 1 and 2 are complete and verified. The remainder of this document
reconstructs how they were built and what design questions the later stages
raise.

## Computing environment

The pipeline runs on Rivanna, the University of Virginia's high-performance
computing cluster. Two constraints motivate this. The chosen model is too large
for commodity hardware and requires several high-memory GPUs held in parallel.
And the full extraction over 58,467 articles is embarrassingly parallel, so it is
partitioned across many workers to complete in tractable wall-clock time. The
orchestration code is written to tolerate preemption and session loss, since
individual jobs run for hours.

# Decision 1: data acquisition

This was the most consequential design axis, and the reasoning is worth
recording in full, because the final architecture was reached only after an
initial approach failed against the empirical realities of the corpus. We began
with one plan, encountered four distinct problems, and converged on a different
and more defensible design.

## The initial approach: bulk local corpus

PLOS distributes an open dataset, allofplos, that provides every PLOS article as
a JATS XML file. We ingested it in full: roughly 391,000 articles, about 9 GB
compressed, held on the cluster. Each file embeds not only the article text but
PLOS's hierarchical subject taxonomy, encoded as nested tags:

```
Biology and life sciences  ->  Psychology  ->  Social psychology
```

The attraction was self-containment. Parse the taxonomy from each file, retain
the psychology articles, and never depend on a network service again. The parser
descended to the subfield directly beneath a "Psychology" node:

```python
def get_psychology_subfields(article):
    """Return the psychology subfield(s) an article is tagged with.
    e.g. Biology > Psychology > Social psychology  ->  ["Social psychology"]
    """
    subfields = []
    for node in article.subject_nodes:
        if node.text == "Psychology":
            # grab the tag(s) nested one level under Psychology
            subfields.extend(child.text for child in node.children)
    return subfields
```

## Problem A: taxonomy schema drift

The first implementation returned zero psychology articles. Diagnosis proceeded
by serializing the raw taxonomy block of several recent articles and inspecting
it. The tags were present, but the container element enclosing them had been
renamed. PLOS annotates each taxonomy block with a type attribute; legacy
articles use the value "Discipline", whereas current articles use "Discipline-v3".
The parser matched the literal string "Discipline" and therefore silently
excluded every modern article.

The remedy was to match any type beginning with "Discipline", covering both
schema generations. The broader lesson, which recurred, is that PLOS's encoding
is not stationary across fifteen years of publishing, so structural assumptions
must be validated against the corpus rather than a single exemplar.

## Problem B: subfield vocabulary mismatch

The brief enumerated five target subfields: social, cognitive, developmental,
clinical, and quantitative psychology. Cross-checking against the corpus surfaced
two mismatches. PLOS's controlled vocabulary contains no term "Quantitative
psychology", so that category would have matched nothing. Conversely, PLOS
employs several subfields the brief did not list, including Experimental
psychology, Psychometrics, Behavior, and Emotions.

Rather than impose a preset list the taxonomy does not honor, we consulted the
project owner, who elected to include all subfields. The design accordingly
became taxonomy-driven: retain every article PLOS files under Psychology and
record whichever subfield term PLOS assigned, irrespective of the original five.
This is faithful to the field's own organization and lets downstream analysis
aggregate or subset by subfield at will. In the finished corpus this yields 23
distinct subfields rather than five.

## Problem C: the 2015 discontinuity

With the taxonomy parsing correctly, we executed the full scan over all 391,000
files and produced a first master index. A routine integrity check, tabulating
the count of psychology articles per year, exposed a discontinuity that no
plausible mechanism could explain as signal:

```
2014: 2,002 articles
2015:    12 articles    <- implausible
2016: 2,100 articles
```

A near-empty year bracketed by full ones is diagnostic of a defect, not a trend,
so we investigated rather than proceeding.

The first hypothesis attributed the gap to date parsing: perhaps 2015 articles
were being misdated and displaced into adjacent years. We falsified this by
constructing a year histogram over all PLOS ONE articles regardless of subject,
which showed 2015 fully populated with correctly dated articles. The articles
existed and were dated; they were simply not being recognized as psychology.

The second hypothesis localized the failure to subject detection in 2015
specifically. We instrumented a per-year comparison between the count of articles
our parser tagged as psychology and the count whose raw tags merely contained the
substring "psycholog":

```
year | total articles | tagged psychology | contains "psycholog"
2014 |      594       |        37         |         38
2015 |      561       |         1         |          1
2016 |      435       |        35         |         35
```

This was decisive. For 2015 even the naive substring search returned essentially
nothing, which meant the articles carried no subject taxonomy at all rather than
taxonomy in an unexpected shape. Serializing the raw taxonomy block of several
2015 articles and tabulating the type attributes across the year confirmed it:
almost every 2015 article contained only

```xml
<article-categories>
  <subj-group subj-group-type="heading">
    <subject>Research Article</subject>
  </subj-group>
</article-categories>
```

a bare document-class heading and no subject taxonomy whatever. The tally was
unambiguous: of 561 sampled 2015 articles, 557 carried no subject tags in their
distributed files, as did roughly 37% of 2013 articles.

The finding is therefore a property of the distributed data, not a coding defect.
PLOS classified these articles in its production systems but, for that interval,
never serialized the taxonomy into the downloadable files. A label that was never
written cannot be read. Uncorrected, this would have voided most of 2015 and a
substantial fraction of 2013, invalidating the Middle stage and any longitudinal
trend traversing that interval.

## The resolution: Solr for discovery

The taxonomy is absent from the distributed files but not from PLOS itself. PLOS
operates a Solr search index that holds the authoritative subject classification
for every article, including those whose files omit it. We therefore inverted the
architecture: use the search index to determine which articles qualify
(discovery), and retain the local files solely for the full text the model must
read. This division of labor, search index for discovery and local corpus for
full text, is in fact the design the original brief proposed before the
bulk-local shortcut was attempted.

## Problem D: query construction

Constructing a correct discovery query required two further corrections, each
isolated by adding one constraint at a time and observing the result count.

First, the index contains far more than whole articles; it also indexes
constituent fragments such as sections and figures. Absent a specific filter,
`doc_type:full`, the query returns several million such fragments rather than
articles. Second, the constraints must be issued as strict filter queries. A
loosely composed query is interpreted permissively by the endpoint and returns
effectively the entire date range rather than the psychology subset.

With both corrections applied, each successive constraint narrows the count
coherently:

```
q=*:* only                  : 3,487,529   (all indexed units, incl. fragments)
+ doc_type:full             :   411,419   (whole articles, all journals)
+ journal:"PLOS ONE"        :   332,150
+ article_type Research     :   313,425
+ date = 2015               :    28,107   (PLOS ONE research articles, 2015)
+ subject Psychology        :     4,346   (2015 psychology, recovered)
```

The operative query is a conjunction of filters:

```python
filters = [
    'doc_type:full',                       # essential: whole articles only
    'journal:"PLOS ONE"',
    'article_type:"Research Article"',
    'subject:"Psychology"',
    f'publication_date:[{year}-01-01T00:00:00Z TO {year}-12-31T23:59:59Z]',
]
```

Under the search-index approach, 2015 recovered from 12 articles to 4,346. The
index returns each subject as a full path, for instance /Biology and life
sciences/Psychology/Cognitive psychology/Language, from which we read the
subfield as the segment immediately following "Psychology", preserving the
semantics of the earlier XML parser.

## Operational issues of note

Two cluster-specific failures also arose, both of the kind that silently consume
time when undocumented.

Batch jobs repeatedly failed with a missing-dependency error despite the software
being installed. The cause is that the conventional command for activating the
software environment behaves differently inside a non-interactive batch job than
in an interactive shell; it appeared to succeed but left the job bound to the
wrong interpreter. The fix invokes the correct interpreter by absolute path,
bypassing activation.

Separately, a long-running preprocessing step launched in a terminal background
was terminated whenever the connection dropped, because the web terminal tears
down its process group at session end. The fix submits that work as a scheduled
job, which executes independently of any terminal. Both fixes are now encoded in
the run scripts.

## Data-quality handling

The pipeline tolerates two specific defects observed in the corpus. One article
file was truncated and unparseable; the scanner logs and skips it rather than
aborting a multi-hour job over a single bad file out of 391,000. And roughly 6%
of the articles returned by the search index, predominantly recent 2025 and 2026
publications, are absent from the local file snapshot and thus have no retrievable
full text; these are flagged and excluded from sampling so the pipeline never
attempts to code an article it cannot read.

# The finished master index

Under the search-index approach the per-year counts are continuous, with no
residual gap:

```python
total: 58,467 psychology articles
by year:
  2010:  853   2014: 4,249   2018: 3,492   2022: 3,761
  2011: 1,886  2015: 4,346   2019: 3,219   2023: 3,761
  2012: 2,481  2016: 3,663   2020: 3,548   2024: 4,249
  2013: 4,478  2017: 3,367   2021: 3,714   2025: 5,009
                                            2026: 2,391 (partial year)
by stage:
  early: 13,947   middle: 18,087   covid: 14,784   post-covid: 11,649
```

The lower 2010 count reflects PLOS ONE's smaller early publication volume, a
genuine feature of the venue rather than an artifact. The 2026 count is partial
because the year is incomplete.

# Decision 2: the pilot sample

Before committing to a full run, the model is exercised on a small batch whose
output is adjudicated by hand. Two properties of the sampling design matter.

The sample is stratified rather than simple random. A simple random draw would be
dominated by high-volume subfields such as social and cognitive psychology and
might omit rarer ones entirely, whereas the point of the pilot is to probe the
model across the full range of writing conventions. We therefore draw two
articles from each subfield present in the index.

The draw is reproducible. It is seeded with a fixed value, so the identical
sample can be regenerated by anyone, which is a precondition for a transparent,
auditable process.

```python
def stratified_sample(articles, per_subfield=2, seed=42):
    rng = random.Random(seed)                     # fixed seed = reproducible
    picked = []
    for subfield in all_subfields(articles):      # every subfield present
        candidates = [a for a in articles if subfield in a.subfields]
        if len(candidates) >= per_subfield:       # skip subfields with too few
            picked += rng.sample(candidates, per_subfield)
    return picked
```

The realized sample comprises 46 articles spanning 23 subfields, among them
Social, Cognitive, and Developmental psychology, Personality, Emotions,
Psychometrics, and Behavior.

# Decision 3: model selection

The brief offered two candidate models, of which one was to be selected:

| | Mistral-7B | Llama-3.3-70B (selected) |
|---|---|---|
| Scale | 7 billion parameters | 70 billion parameters |
| Structured-extraction accuracy | Lower; more prone to omission and fabrication | Higher; more reliable |
| Compute cost | Modest; runs on limited hardware | Substantial; requires multiple high-end GPUs |

We selected Llama-3.3-70B. Accuracy is the binding criterion, because an omitted
or fabricated demographic value propagates directly into the reporting-rate
estimates that constitute the study's output. Executing on Rivanna removes the
compute-cost consideration that would otherwise favor the smaller model. The
pilot exists precisely to test whether this selection is warranted before the
full run.

# Extraction mechanics

Each article's text is submitted to the model with an instruction that fixes both
the extraction targets and the output format:

```text
You are coding a psychology research article for a systematic review of
demographic reporting. For EACH distinct participant sample, extract:
 - gender: reported? (0/1) and percentage breakdown (male/female/other)
 - race:   reported? (0/1) and percentage breakdown (white/black/hispanic/asian/other)
 - education: reported? (0/1) and percentage with vs. without college
 - socioeconomic status: 0 = not reported, 1 = words only, 2 = a specific number

Respond with ONLY a JSON array, one element per sample, with these exact keys...
```

Two safeguards constrain the output. It is schema-validated, so a response must
be well-formed structured data carrying exactly the required fields; malformed
output is rejected and flagged rather than silently admitted to the dataset. And
the methods and participants sections are reordered to the front of the submitted
text, since demographics are reported there, which concentrates the relevant
signal near the start of the prompt for long articles.

# Scaling the full run

Executing 58,467 articles through a 70-billion-parameter model is
compute-intensive. The pipeline partitions the work into independent shards
executed concurrently across many GPUs. Each shard writes its own output file,
and the run is idempotent under restart: an interrupted shard skips the articles
it has already completed and resumes, which is essential for multi-hour jobs
subject to preemption.

# Aggregation and inference

Given the completed demographics table, the final stage computes, for each
demographic and each year, and separately for each of the four stages, two
quantities. The reporting rate is the proportion of samples reporting a given
demographic. The mean composition is, for example, the average percentage female
among samples that reported gender. Tracing these across 2010 to 2026 constitutes
the study's answer: whether demographic reporting in psychology is improving, and
how the trajectory differs across the early, middle, COVID, and post-COVID
periods.

# Reproducibility

All code and documentation is version-controlled on GitHub (repository
SJ-Jain-systems/Halle). Each stage is an independent, testable module:

```
src/
  solr_client.py          discovery via the PLOS Solr search index
  build_index_solr.py     materialize the master index of 58,467 articles
  jats_xml.py             parse metadata and full text from the article files
  sample_articles.py      draw the stratified pilot sample
  extract_demographics.py the model instruction and schema validation
  model_backend.py        model execution on the GPUs (vLLM / transformers)
  run_pipeline.py         full run, sharded and restartable
  analyze_trends.py       reporting-rate aggregation by year and stage
docs/
  DECISIONS.md            the three decisions, with full reasoning
  RUNNING_ON_RIVANNA.md   step-by-step run instructions for the cluster
  SCORING_RUBRIC.md       the pilot adjudication rubric
scripts/                  the diagnostics that isolated the 2015 gap and more
tests/                    33 automated tests over the non-model logic
```

Two points bear emphasis for anyone auditing the work. The non-model logic is
covered by 33 automated tests spanning parsing, filtering, sampling, and
aggregation; the model itself is validated by manual adjudication of the pilot.
And the diagnostic scripts that isolated the schema drift and the 2015 gap are
retained in the repository, so the evidentiary basis for each design decision
remains inspectable.

# Open questions for discussion

Three decisions would benefit from input before the full run.

1. Subfield scope. PLOS's taxonomy yields 23 psychology subfields, some broad
   (Behavior, Emotions) and some tangential to human-participant research
   (for example animal-behavior work filed under Psychology). Do we analyze all
   23, or restrict to a defined core of human-participant subfields, and if so
   which?

2. Coverage at the interval boundaries. Pre-2011 articles use the older tagging
   generation, and a fraction of 2025 to 2026 articles lack local full text. Are
   the earliest and latest years complete enough to support a fair longitudinal
   comparison, or should the analysis window be bounded (for instance 2011 to
   2024)?

3. Validation threshold. What level of pilot accuracy, measured against the
   scoring rubric, justifies proceeding to the full run, and who performs the
   manual adjudication?
